rules_text:
Rules summary The goal in Oust is to completely clear the board of enemy stones, to oust your opponent - a paradox since the board is empty to begin with. Your opponent has to add at least one stone before you can capture all of their stones. Non-capturing placements: A non-capturing placement either forms no connections (adjacencies) with any stones, or forms one or more connections only with enemy stones. A noncapturing placement does not form any connections with stones of its own color. Capturing placements: When you place a stone which forms one or more connections with your own groups, you create a new, larger group of your own stones. You can only make such a placement if said new group will have one or more connections with enemy groups upon its creation and if all said enemy groups are smaller than said new group. Upon making such a placement, all said enemy groups are removed from the board. Multiple placements per turn: After capturing one or more enemy groups and while it is still your turn, you must continue to add stones until you make a non-capturing placement, at which time your turn is concluded. Pie rule: on their first turn only, the second player may choose to play as the first player instead of making a regular move.

[Rating: 2/10] The game should have been called "Hopeless". It's not a good feeling to see so many bad moves.

[Rating: 3/10] This feels like another kind of parity game, with the object being to stall until your opponent is forced to let you gobble up one of his stones and start a snowball effect that decides the game. I could be entirely wrong as I only played the square version on Igfip and I don't think the bot is any good.  Now I've tried the hex version and still didn't find the game that others seem to be commenting on. You place a few stones until you run out of safe spots and the rest is pretty much a foregone conclusion? Presumably the board was much too small but I don't see any charm in the gameplay.

[Rating: 4/10] Not sure about this.  Chances are, this game is deeper than I am :-)  Might have missed something, but (playing on a 7-hex hexagon) it seemed like once you got ahead, you were hard to catch.  Might be like Go in that regard, but the smaller board means you pay for mistakes faster, and in a more obvious fashion.  Similar system to Explosion?

[Rating: 4/10] Oust isn't a bad game, however I felt like there was only one major swing in the whole game. The rest was merely going through the motions or arbitrary build up. Would much rather play Circle of Life which feels inspired by Oust

[Rating: 4/10] Another 2 player abstract based around stalling until you run out of viable moves and then you either have your pieces eaten or do the eating. Might be some more advance strategy worth experiencing and thinking about, but I don't feel compelled to do that at the moment.

[Rating: 5/10] Oust is not a particularly easy game to wrap my head around. It's an elimination game on a board that begins empty. I've only played the hexagonal grid version, which most commenters seem to prefer. It works OK, and the subtle build up of group strength feels like a brinksmanship sort of arms race. That said, I didn't enjoy the experience very much, partly because it's so cold and partly because the denouement lasted a bit too long.
